name: Daniel

seo.title: Daniel the Prophet: his life, the lions' den and his visions
seo.description: Daniel in plain words: the king's food, the dreams, the writing on the wall, the lions' den, his prayer, his feast days and the myths.

band.lede: Taken from Judah to Babylon as a young man, he explained the dreams of kings. He kept on praying when the law forbade it, and was thrown to the lions.

who: Daniel was a young man of Judah, taken to Babylon. He rose high at the court of its kings, and of Persia's after them. He explained Nebuchadnezzar's dreams and the writing on the wall. He kept praying three times a day when the law forbade it, and God shut the lions' mouths.

tidbits.text: Josephus says Alexander the Great was shown the book of Daniel, where a Greek would destroy the Persian empire. Alexander “supposed that himself was the person intended.”
In the Hebrew Bible, the angels **Gabriel** and **Michael** are named only in Daniel. Gabriel comes back in Luke, to Zechariah and to Mary. Michael comes back in Jude and Revelation.

In Greek, Susanna's trial turns on puns. The elder who names a mastic tree, a *schinos*, will be cut, *schisei*, in two. Julius Africanus told Origen the puns showed the story was first written in Greek. Origen was “still in doubt”.

The young men's song in the fire is one of the Greek chapters. The Church of England's *Book of Common Prayer* sets it at Morning Prayer, as the Benedicite: “O all ye Works of the Lord, bless ye the Lord”.

cite.text: Daniel 3:57-90 in Catholic Bibles; the *Book of Common Prayer*, Morning Prayer

facts.label: Name
facts.text: **Daniel** means **God is my judge**. At court he was renamed **Belteshazzar**, “after the name of my god”, said Nebuchadnezzar. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* reads it as **Bel protect his life**.

facts.label: From
facts.text: **Judah**. He was one of the young men taken from “the royal family and the nobility”. Josephus says he and his three friends were kin of **Zedekiah**, the last king of Judah.

facts.label: Taken
facts.text: To **Babylon**, by **Nebuchadnezzar**, in the third year of King Jehoiakim. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* dates it to **605 BC**, when he was probably about **fourteen**.

facts.label: Served
facts.text: Four kings: **Nebuchadnezzar**, **Belshazzar**, **Darius the Mede** and **Cyrus** the Persian. When Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians, he kept his high place.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: The Bible names **no wife or children**. A Jewish tradition, accepted by many Fathers, held that he was made a **eunuch** at court. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* notes the text does not say so.

facts.label: Wrote
facts.text: The **book of Daniel**. Chapters 1 to 6 tell of him. Chapters 7 to 12 are **four visions**, in his own words. When it was written is argued over: see below.

facts.label: Languages
facts.text: Two. His book is in **Hebrew**, with **Aramaic** from chapter 2 verse 4 to the end of chapter 7. The switch comes mid-verse, when the king's astrologers answer him “in Aramaic”.

facts.label: Greek chapters
facts.text: **Catholic** and **Orthodox** Bibles hold three more pieces, kept in Greek: the **prayer and song** of the three young men in the fire, **Susanna**, and **Bel and the Dragon**. The Hebrew Bible and most Protestant Bibles leave them out.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: No one knows. One tradition says in the **royal vault** at Babylon. The rabbis said he went home to **Jerusalem**. Since at least the 1100s, his tomb has been shown at **Susa**, in Persia.

facts.label: In art
facts.text: In the **lions' den**, praying among the lions. On the **Sistine Chapel** ceiling, Michelangelo painted him among the prophets, with a great book.

quotes.who: God's word to the proud king of Tyre, through Ezekiel, a prophet of the same exile. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* takes this to be our Daniel. The 1911 *Britannica* thought Ezekiel meant an older, famous Daniel.

quotes.q: He did not only prophesy of future events, as did the other prophets, but he also determined the time of their accomplishment.

moments.title: The king's food
moments.text: Nebuchadnezzar took Jerusalem and carried off young men “from the royal family and the nobility”. For three years they would learn the language and literature of the Chaldeans. Among them were Daniel, Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah. They were given new names: Belteshazzar, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Daniel “made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king's food or wine.” He asked the steward for a test. “Please test your servants for ten days. Let us be given only vegetables to eat and water to drink.” After ten days they looked healthier than all the rest. In time the king found them “ten times better than all the magicians and enchanters in his entire kingdom.”

moments.title: Susanna
moments.text: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles tell of a young Daniel in the story of Susanna. She was the wife of Joakim, “a very fair woman, and one who feared the Lord.” Two elders, made judges that year, lusted after her. They caught her alone in her garden and told her to lie with them, or they would swear a young man had been with her. She refused: “It is better for me to fall into your hands, and not do it, than to sin in the sight of the Lord.” The people believed the elders, and she was led away to die. Then Daniel cried out, “Are you all such fools, you sons of Israel, that without examination or knowledge of the truth you have condemned a daughter of Israel?” He questioned the elders apart. He asked each under which tree he had seen her. One said a mastic tree, the other an oak. Their own words convicted them, and Susanna was saved.

cite.text: Susanna (Daniel 13 in Catholic Bibles), World English Bible

moments.title: The king's dream
moments.text: Nebuchadnezzar had dreams that troubled him. He ordered his wise men to tell him the dream itself, and then what it meant. They could not. “No one on earth can do what the king requests!” So he ordered every wise man in Babylon put to death, Daniel and his friends among them. Daniel asked the king for time, and asked his friends to plead with God for mercy. That night the mystery was revealed to him in a vision. He told the king his dream: a great statue, with a head of gold, a chest of silver, a belly of bronze, legs of iron, and feet part iron and part clay. A stone was “cut out, but not by human hands.” It struck the statue's feet, and became a mountain that filled the whole earth. Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face before Daniel, and made him ruler over the province of Babylon.

moments.title: The tree cut down
moments.text: Chapter 4 is told by Nebuchadnezzar himself, as a letter to every nation. He dreamed of a great tree cut down to its stump, and called for Daniel. Daniel was alarmed at what it meant. “My lord,” he said, “may the dream apply to those who hate you, and its interpretation to your enemies!” But he told him the truth. The king would be driven away to live with the beasts, until he knew that the Most High rules over the kingdoms of men. Twelve months later, the king walked on his palace roof and boasted, “Is this not Babylon the Great, which I myself have built”. While the words were still in his mouth, a voice came from heaven. He was driven away, and ate grass like an ox. At the end of those days he looked up to heaven, and his sanity was restored. “Now I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise and exalt and glorify the King of heaven”.

moments.title: The writing on the wall
moments.text: King Belshazzar held a feast for a thousand of his nobles. They drank from the gold and silver vessels taken from the temple in Jerusalem, and praised their gods of gold and silver. At that moment the fingers of a human hand wrote on the plaster of the wall. The king's knees knocked together. None of his wise men could read it. The queen remembered Daniel. “There is a man in your kingdom who has the spirit of the holy gods in him.” Daniel, by now an old man, read the words: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN. God had numbered the days of the king's reign. “You have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.” His kingdom would go to the Medes and Persians. “That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain”.

moments.title: Three times a day
moments.text: Darius the Mede made Daniel one of three men over the kingdom's governors, and planned to set him over the whole kingdom. The others looked for a charge against him, and found none. “We will never find any charge against this Daniel unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.” So they had the king sign a decree. For thirty days, anyone who prayed to any god or man but the king would be thrown to the lions. Daniel went home. In his upper room, with the windows open toward Jerusalem, he knelt three times a day and prayed, “just as he had done before.” The king tried until sundown to save him, but his own law could not be changed. “May your God, Whom you serve continually, deliver you!” A stone was sealed over the mouth of the den, and the king spent the night fasting. What he found at dawn is told below, with the wonders.

moments.title: One like the Son of Man
moments.text: Daniel dreamed of four great beasts coming up out of the sea, each different from the others. Then thrones were set in place, “and the Ancient of Days took His seat.” His clothing was white as snow. “I saw One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven.” He was given a kingdom, and “His kingdom is one that will never be destroyed.” Daniel's face turned pale. “But I kept the matter to myself.” Jesus took these words for His own. At His trial, the high priest asked if He was the Christ. He answered, “I am,” and added, “you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming with the clouds of heaven.” The high priest tore his clothes.

moments.title: Seventy years
moments.text: Daniel read in the prophet Jeremiah that the ruin of Jerusalem would last seventy years. So he turned to God “by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.” He confessed his people's sins as his own: his prayer is below. “While I was still praying,” the angel Gabriel came to him in swift flight, about the time of the evening sacrifice. An answer had gone out at the start of his prayer, Gabriel said, “for you are highly precious.” Then he told him of seventy weeks decreed for his people and his city, until “the Messiah, the Prince”. What the weeks mean has been argued over ever since.

moments.title: Footprints in the ashes
moments.text: In Bel and the Dragon, Daniel lives at the court of Cyrus the Persian. Every day the Babylonians gave their idol Bel twelve great measures of flour, forty sheep and six firkins of wine. The king asked Daniel why he did not worship it. “Don't you see how much he eats and drinks every day?” Daniel laughed. “O king, don't be deceived; for this is just clay inside, and brass outside, and never ate or drank anything.” The food was set out and the temple sealed with the king's ring. Daniel had his servants scatter ashes over the floor. In the morning the food was gone, and Daniel laughed again. “Behold now the pavement, and mark well whose footsteps these are.” The priests had come in by a secret door with their wives and children, and eaten it all.

cite.text: Bel and the Dragon 1-22 (Daniel 14 in Catholic Bibles), World English Bible

moments.title: The man in linen
moments.text: Daniel mourned for three full weeks, with no rich food, meat or wine. Then, on the bank of the Tigris, he saw “a certain man dressed in linen”. His face was “like the brilliance of lightning”. The men with Daniel ran and hid, and he fell to the ground. A hand touched him and set him trembling on his hands and knees. “Do not be afraid, Daniel,” the man said. His words had been heard from the first day. But “the prince of the kingdom of Persia opposed me for twenty-one days,” until Michael came to help. “Peace be with you! Be strong now; be very strong!”

miracles.lede: The book tells of no wonder done by Daniel's own hand. It tells of wonders God did for him and for his friends. He was quick to say where the power came from:

pledge.q: No wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery of which he inquires. But there is a God in heaven Who reveals mysteries.

feature.title: times he was thrown to the lions

items.title: The mouths of the lions
items.text: The king had sealed the den with his own ring. At the first light of dawn he hurried to it, and cried out in anguish. “O Daniel, servant of the living God, has your God, Whom you serve continually, been able to deliver you from the lions?” Daniel answered from the den.
items.quote: My God sent His angel and shut the mouths of the lions. They have not hurt me, for I was found innocent in His sight.
items.witness: They lifted him out, and no wounds whatsoever were found on him, “because he had trusted in his God.” Darius wrote to every nation that men must fear “the God of Daniel”.

items.when: Six days, in the Greek chapters
items.title: Seven lions, and a dinner
items.text: Daniel killed a great dragon the Babylonians worshipped. He fed it lumps of pitch, fat and hair, and it burst. “The king has become a Jew,” the people said, and they made the king hand Daniel over. He was thrown into a den of seven lions, left unfed so they would devour him. In Judea, the prophet Habakkuk was taking stew and bread to his reapers. The angel of the Lord lifted him “by the hair of his head” and set him in Babylon, over the den. “O Daniel, Daniel, take the dinner which God has sent you.”
items.quote: You have remembered me, O God! You haven't forsaken those who love You!
items.witness: On the seventh day the king came to mourn for him, and found Daniel sitting there. From Bel and the Dragon, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

cite.text: Bel and the Dragon 23-42 (Daniel 14 in Catholic Bibles), World English Bible

more.title: The fourth man in the fire
more.text: This is his three friends' story, and Daniel is not in it. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego would not bow to the king's golden statue. Their God was able to save them, they told him. “But even if He does not, let it be known to you, O king, that we will not serve your gods or worship the golden statue you have set up.” The furnace was heated seven times hotter, and they were thrown in, bound. Then the king jumped up in amazement. When they came out, “Not a hair of their heads was singed”. Catholic and Orthodox Bibles add the prayer and the song they sang in the flames.
more.quote: I see four men, unbound and unharmed, walking around in the fire—and the fourth looks like a son of the gods!

words.note: He left no letters. Chapters 7 to 12 of his book are in his own voice, and the stories before them keep his words. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible. The Greek chapters and 1 Maccabees are from the World English Bible, named where they stand.

feature.kicker: The night the dream was revealed
feature.q: Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and power belong to Him. He changes the times and seasons; He removes kings and establishes them. He gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to the discerning. He reveals the deep and hidden things; He knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with Him.
feature.ctx: The king had ordered every wise man in Babylon put to death. During the night the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, “and he blessed the God of heaven”.

quotes.q: Break away from your sins by doing what is right, and from your iniquities by showing mercy to the oppressed.
quotes.who: To Nebuchadnezzar, the most powerful king on earth, after telling him his dream of the tree.

quotes.q: You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else. Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him.
quotes.who: To Belshazzar, who had offered him purple robes, a gold chain and the third place in his kingdom.

quotes.q: Speak, my lord, for you have strengthened me.
quotes.who: To the man in linen, whose touch had given him back his strength.

quotes.q: Because I may not honor idols made with hands, but only the living God, Who has created the sky and the earth, and has sovereignty over all flesh.
quotes.who: To King Cyrus, who asked why he did not worship Bel. From Bel and the Dragon, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles.

cite.text: Bel and the Dragon 5, World English Bible

prayer.title: His prayer
prayer.intro: He prayed it in sackcloth and ashes, after reading Jeremiah's seventy years. It confesses his people's sins as his own, and it ends like this:
prayer.q: So now, our God, hear the prayers and petitions of Your servant. For Your sake, O Lord, cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate sanctuary. Incline Your ear, O my God, and hear; open Your eyes and see the desolation of the city that bears Your name. For we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion. O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act! For Your sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people bear Your name.

myths.claim: Daniel was a young man in the lions' den.
myths.truth: He was taken to Babylon as a youth, probably about fourteen, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*. The lions' den came decades later, after Babylon fell to the Medes and Persians. By the night of the writing on the wall, the same encyclopedia reckons, he was “now at least eighty years of age”.

myths.claim: Daniel was thrown into the fiery furnace.
myths.truth: That was his three friends, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego. Daniel is not named in the chapter, and the book does not say where he was. Later Jewish stories explained that the king had sent him away, says the *Catholic Encyclopedia*, knowing he would never bow to the statue.

As a young man he asked for vegetables and water, so as not to defile himself with the king's food and wine. Decades later he tells of three weeks of mourning: “I ate no rich food, no meat or wine entered my mouth”. So the meat and wine he gave up then were a fast, not a rule for life.

The king did call him “chief of the magicians”. But Daniel told Nebuchadnezzar that no magician could reveal his dream: only God could. Cyril of Jerusalem, a bishop of the 300s, said the king was right that the Holy Spirit was in him, “but he was not the master of the magicians, for he was no magician, but was wise through the Holy Ghost.”

cite.text: Daniel 2:27-28; 4:9; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechetical Lectures*, Lecture 16

myths.claim: Daniel is one of the Prophets in the Hebrew Bible.
myths.truth: Christian Bibles put Daniel among the prophets, after Ezekiel. The Hebrew Bible does not. It places his book in its third part, the Writings, “between Ezra and Esther”, as the 1911 *Britannica* puts it. Jesus still called him “the prophet Daniel”, and Josephus called him “one of the greatest of the prophets”.

cite.text: Matthew 24:15; Josephus, *Antiquities*, book 10, chapter 11; the 1911 *Britannica*, “Daniel, Book of”

extras.title: When was it written?
extras.lede: Daniel's visions grow more and more detailed as they come down to one king: Antiochus IV Epiphanes, who ruled from 175 to 164 BC and tried to stamp out the worship of the LORD. Was the book written by Daniel in the exile, or by a later author in the days of Antiochus? The question is very old. Here each side speaks for itself.

items.title: Porphyry's attack
items.text: Porphyry, a pagan philosopher who wrote against the Christians, gave the twelfth book of his work to Daniel. Jerome sums up his case. Porphyry denied that the book was written by Daniel,
items.quote: but rather by some individual living in Judaea at the time of the Antiochus who was surnamed Epiphanes.

cite.text: Jerome, *Commentary on Daniel*, prologue, tr. Gleason Archer

items.title: Jerome's answer
items.text: Jerome answered that the attack proved the point. Porphyry had seen how exactly the prophecies came true, and could not deny it.
items.quote: But this very attack testifies to Daniel's accuracy. For so striking was the reliability of what the prophet foretold, that he could not appear to unbelievers as a predicter of the future, but rather a narrator of things already past.

cite.text: Jerome, *Commentary on Daniel*, prologue, tr. Gleason Archer

items.title: By Daniel, in the exile
items.text: This is the traditional view, held by Jews and Christians for most of history. Its first witness is Jesus, Who spoke of “the prophet Daniel”. Josephus tells that the book was shown to Alexander the Great, and 1 Maccabees already knows its stories. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* of 1908 sums it up:
items.quote: Christian tradition, both in the East and in the West, has been practically unanimous from Christ's time to the present day in admitting the genuineness of the Book of Daniel.

cite.text: Matthew 24:15; 1 Maccabees 2:59-60; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Book of Daniel”

items.title: In the days of Antiochus
items.text: Most modern scholars date the book to the reign of Antiochus. They point to its late Hebrew, to Persian and Greek words in it, and to visions that are exact up to Antiochus and go astray after him. Jesus, says the 1911 *Britannica*, was simply naming a book by its usual title. It added:
items.quote: The Book of Daniel loses none of its beauty and force because we are bound, in the light of modern criticism, to consider it as a production of the reign of Antiochus Epiphanes.

cite.text: The 1911 *Britannica*, “Daniel, Book of”; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Book of Daniel”

circle.name: Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah
circle.text: His three friends from Judah, trained with him at court. Babylon called them **Shadrach**, **Meshach** and **Abednego**. When the king ordered the wise men killed, Daniel asked them to plead with God for mercy. At his request they were set over the province of Babylon. Their own story is the fiery furnace.

circle.name: Nebuchadnezzar
circle.text: King of Babylon, who took Jerusalem and carried Daniel off. He fell on his face before Daniel, and later ate grass like an ox. His last words in the book praise “the King of heaven”.

circle.name: Belshazzar
circle.text: King at Babylon's last feast, who drank from the temple's vessels. He was slain the night Daniel read the writing on the wall.

circle.name: Darius the Mede
circle.text: He received the kingdom at sixty-two, and set Daniel high in it. Tricked into signing the decree, he fasted all night, and ran to the den at dawn.

circle.name: Cyrus the Persian
circle.text: Daniel prospered in his reign. In the Greek chapters it is Cyrus who asks him why he will not worship Bel.

circle.name: Ashpenaz
circle.text: Chief of Nebuchadnezzar's court officials. He gave the four young men their new names, and God gave Daniel “favor and compassion” in his eyes.

circle.name: Arioch
circle.text: Commander of the king's guard, sent to put the wise men to death. Daniel answered him “with discretion and tact”, and Arioch brought him to the king.

circle.name: The queen
circle.text: She remembered Daniel when no one could read the writing on the wall, and told the king to send for him.

circle.name: Gabriel
circle.text: The angel who explained his visions. He came to him in swift flight while he was still praying.

circle.name: Susanna
circle.text: The woman he saved from a false charge, in the Greek chapters.

circle.name: Habakkuk
circle.text: The prophet an angel carried from Judea to bring Daniel his dinner in the lions' den, in the Greek chapters.

death.title: How the record leaves him
death.big: The Bible tells no death. Its last words to him are a promise of rest, and of rising again.
paras: The last date his book gives is the third year of Cyrus king of Persia. By the Tigris, Daniel saw his last vision.
He did not understand all of it, and asked what the end would be. “Go on your way, Daniel,” came the answer, “for the words are closed up and sealed until the time of the end.”

The Coptic synaxarium says he “remained in Babylon for seventy years, then departed in peace.” The OCA says he lived to old age and died in captivity. Rome's book of martyrs keeps his day “At Babylon”.

items.q: My lord, what will be the outcome of these things?

items.k: The book's last words to him
items.q: But as for you, go on your way until the end. You will rest, and then you will arise to your inheritance at the end of the days.

later.title: A coffin on a chain
later.text: About 1165, the Jewish traveller Benjamin of Tudela was shown Daniel's tomb at Susa, in Persia. He heard that the two halves of the city had fought over the coffin, and agreed to keep it a year each. Then Sinjar, the sultan of Persia, had it put in a coffin of crystal and hung from the middle of the bridge. “And to this very day the coffin is suspended from the bridge.” A tomb of Daniel is still shown near Susa.

cite.text: Benjamin of Tudela, *Itinerary*, tr. Marcus Nathan Adler (1907); Catholic Encyclopedia, “Daniel”

saint.big: Yes. He is honoured as a saint in the Orthodox and Catholic calendars. The Orthodox keep his day with his three friends, on 17 December.

churches.note: Church of England and Episcopal Church

paras: The Orthodox also remember him on the two Sundays before Christmas, the Sunday of the Holy Forefathers and the Sunday of the Holy Fathers, says the OCA.
They sing of him and his three friends on their day. Rome's book of martyrs, in its 1916 edition, gives him one line:

quotes.q: Great are the achievements of faith! In the fountain of flame, as by the water of rest, the three holy youths rejoiced. And the prophet Daniel was shown a shepherd of lions, as of sheep. By their prayers, O Christ God, save our souls!

kin.name: Joseph
kin.text: Another young Hebrew who rose at a foreign court by reading the king's dreams. He too gave God the credit. “I myself cannot do it,” he told Pharaoh, “but God will give Pharaoh a sound answer.”

kin.name: Esther
kin.text: A Jew at the Persian court who, like Daniel, faced a king's law. She went in to the king, “even though it is against the law. And if I perish, I perish!”

kin.name: Nehemiah
kin.text: Cupbearer to a Persian king. Like Daniel, he fasted and confessed his people's sins as his own before he asked God for anything. “Both I and my father's house have sinned.”
